message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to different orders—lions to **Carnivora** (suborder Feliformia) and zebras to **Perissodactyla** (suborder Equoidea). Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes many modern groups such as carnivores, ungulates, bats, and whales.

In terms of evolutionary history, the last common ancestor of the families Felidae (cats) and Equidae (horses, donkeys, zebras) would have been a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly 60–70 million years ago during the Paleogene period. This ancestor would have possessed the basic mammalian body plan (four limbs, hair, mammary glands, etc.) but would have lacked the specialized features seen in modern cats (sharp retractable claws, carnassial teeth) or horses (high‑crowned molars adapted for grazing).

So, while lions and zebras share a very distant common ancestor—a small, early placental mammal from the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene—they diverged into distinct lineages long before the appearance of the modern species we see today.
